title: After Studying at Johns Hopkins Hospital
paragraphs: This time, from March 26 to May 26, I did a nine-week clinical clerkship in gastroenterology and anesthesiology at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore, USA. A clinical clerkship abroad in my sixth year had been a vague goal since I entered the university, and now that I have actually been sent and have returned to Japan after the nine weeks that I thought would be long are over, it feels like it was a single moment. Over these nearly two months, I am grateful to everyone in the International Collaboration Office and the Student Affairs Office, and to my parents who supported this study abroad. Below I briefly write down my impressions and thoughts based on this study abroad.

Preparation for the study abroad began with TOEFL preparation, but what differs from the tests we have taken so far, such as the TOEIC, is that output-type sections such as Speaking and Writing are required. In Speaking in particular, you have to deal in a short time with questions that are difficult to think about and answer even in Japanese, and when I started studying I could not speak at all. I thought I was good at English, but if you cannot express what you are thinking, nothing gets across, and English at that level can never be called usable English. On this study abroad too I had many opportunities to realise the importance of the ability to express oneself, and I think I should have done more of this output training from the time of studying for the TOEFL. For Speaking, I practised for nearly a year, like batting practice, with sets of six test questions published on YouTube and elsewhere. I think the best strategy for Speaking is to increase your repertoire of answer patterns, so I recommend this way of studying. For the other sections I did no particular preparation, but getting used to the test format is an important point for the TOEFL as a whole, so I think it is very important to get used to the computer-based format with the official problem sets, and to get used to the atmosphere of the venue and the speed of the test by taking the real test.

After the destination is decided, what matters is preparing documents and negotiating with the local side, and it is good to do so in cooperation with the professors of the International Collaboration Office and, if there is someone going with you, that person. Please proceed carefully. Deciding the clerkship department is often a big obstacle for studying abroad, but mine was decided relatively early, in January of this year, so I was able to narrow down my studying to some extent. However, even there I was asked, for example, to differentiate suspected gastrointestinal bleeding from various anemias for a drop in Hb, so it may be important for a study abroad to broaden your knowledge, even if shallowly, on the basis of medical vocabulary, regardless of department, and it will surely be useful for your own future, so I would like you to try it. I have so little vocabulary that I have never finished a whole vocabulary book, but I felt that, whatever one does in everyday conversation, in medical conversation, if you do not know the medical words as tools, you cannot even prepare alternative expressions and the conversation does not move forward, so acquiring many words is very important and an important starting line.

Locally, I first spent about a month in gastroenterology. Gastroenterology has three divisions, the GI consult team, the GI inpatient team and the Liver service (Hepatology), and I spent two weeks in the liver service and a little under three weeks in the consult team. In the liver service, mornings were conference and ward rounds, and in the afternoon we did consults for inpatients who showed abnormal liver enzymes. Liver inpatients included patients with every kind of liver damage, such as alcoholic and drug-induced, and my impression was that the alcoholic type was especially common. At JHH, liver transplant surgeries are performed nearly every week, and I remember being greatly surprised that inpatients were registered on the transplant list one after another. I was also allowed to attend the weekly conference that decides who gets a transplant, and it was quite interesting to see patients being evaluated, with opinions from various professions, from every aspect, such as medical background, living situation, work and family environment, as to whether transplant treatment would actually improve the prognosis, and it was a good opportunity to see multidisciplinary cooperation. In the consult service, we did a preliminary examination of the patient at noon, then presented at the attending rounds in the afternoon, decided the treatment plan and wrote in the chart. Of course, students do not prescribe on their own, but when I first presented on the first Tuesday, I did not know whether I was supposed to do various things on my own, so I wrote a summary like a chart note and sent it to the fellow, and the next day the attending said to me, "Where is your note from yesterday?" and I thought "I can write these freely!", and after my account was opened I wrote many notes. As is true of JHH as a whole, most of the doctors did not mind teaching, and all said "It's best for you to learn the way you want to learn," which I was very grateful for. In the overall GI consult, I went from watching endoscopy in the morning to the preliminary examination, and then attending rounds and charting in the afternoon. The process of discussing the preliminary examination results with the fellow and deciding the recommended treatment was very educational, and I also remember being given various materials by the fellow, who said these would be useful. It was surprising that they remembered the appropriate manuals, guidelines and papers and could produce them immediately. In the overall GI consult, the symptoms were diverse and the organs to be considered at the same time increased greatly, but by following the flow of seeing the consult patient and doing the endoscopy the next day, I could see the series of treatments within the quick flow of treating inpatients. I do regret that I could have been more proactive in follow-up afterward, so I hope my juniors will follow up on their patients even after they leave their hands.

The anesthesiology department had a considerably well-established division for accepting students, and the teaching system was also very well organised. In anesthesia, even a single operation allows you to view the patient in a truly multifaceted way, so even if studying for the national examination covers it all only shallowly, each element (pharmacology, respiratory system and so on) is a very deep field, and being able to learn from the residents' explanations and the background of each procedure and medication was a very good study for me, who had regarded anesthesia as something vague, and I think it was a good experience to become able to propose something, even if little, following those criteria. As for the technical side too, I was told "Have they said you can touch patients? Then go ahead and do it!" and I did many procedures proactively. Personally, being allowed to do not only clinical reasoning but also skills in anesthesiology was a very good experience. I realised that whether or not you have done a clinical procedure such as intubation makes a complete difference starting from your mindset, and being able to experience various procedures multiple times before becoming a resident gave me a certain amount of confidence. As for the range of procedures, when I asked classmates who had actually rotated through anesthesia in the second polyclinic clerkship at Nagoya University, it seemed to me that I had been able to do about the same, but since there were frequently people with obesity, which is also a social problem in the US, besides technical difficulty there were many points to be careful about in anesthesia planning too, and discussions about them with the residents and attendings taught me a lot. I also had two night shifts, and the experience of night shifts themselves and being able to see patients rarely seen in Japan, such as stab wound patients, was a valuable opportunity gained from the study abroad. The residents basically change every week, and when there were night shifts or conferences someone else took charge, so I spent much effort in the first hour or so telling someone who did not know me at all how much I knew and what skills I had done, but since the other party also cannot take the next step unless they know your level, I would like my juniors to promote themselves in whatever department they go to, with the feeling that it is better to do so and fail a little than to do nothing. It may not be good to say it is fine to fail, but being able to avoid fearing failure is a privilege of students.

Before getting to the summary, let me take one break. America is a society where whoever speaks up wins, or in other words, a society where you lose if you do not speak up. For example, when I opened my account for the chart, there was a problem and I could not use the account for the first three days. The help desk did not help much, but after I asked over and over by phone and sent many emails, they finally opened my account. At the Amtrak ticket desk, at the NY Hilton room and elsewhere too, I made a big fuss saying "No, no, this is wrong," but if you feel "I don't like this," "This is strange," or "This is wrong," please make a fuss first. If you do not, they will not even begin to deal with you. In the hospital and at tourist spots alike, in that world, being proactive is important in everything. With the feeling that you are only a one-time visitor anyway, please try to persuade the other party so that you get closer to what you want to do.

Now, I learned many things through this study abroad, but I think the biggest was "how good the environment in Japan is." First, with Japanese medicine, even if advanced medicine cannot be provided in some cases because of insurance and so on, the level of care required by many people is not at all inferior to America, and it has good points such as patients' living backgrounds being reasonably stable. If you divide people into ten levels, I think America is an environment that produces many 10s who achieve tremendous success, but at the same time it is an extreme environment that also produces many 1s who are beyond help. Because things that are unthinkable in Japan, in terms of social background, insurance and housing, happen as a matter of course, there were cases where medical care lost its effect because of social factors, for example restrictions on the drugs that could be used or compliance problems. Noticing the wonder of what we take for granted, the environment in which we can receive medical care in Japan, was also something unique to studying abroad. On the other hand, I also felt that Japan's good environment is sometimes like lukewarm water. At JHH, among the signs written in the languages of various countries there was no Japanese, and there are very few Japanese even among the staff. I feel that Japan's presence in America and the world is declining. Recently there has been a lot of talk that Japan's expansion overseas is lagging behind Asian countries such as China and Korea, but the fact that Japan is such a wonderful environment that one does not have to take on America may, in a sense, be breeding complacency. The doctors from China, Korea and India come with the determination to abandon their own countries and change their lives, so I think it is more accurate to say that we Japanese are unavoidably beaten by their tremendous drive than that Japanese are inferior. I do not think going abroad is only good, but the reality is perhaps that we have not fully made use of the good aspects of Japan's environment and have not sold them. Speaking only of students, it is said that for a study abroad you should "make an effort to be given inpatients to be in charge of!", but as for whether I had such an attitude in the first polyclinic clerkship in Japan, I did not at all. I indulged in the lukewarm lectures of the first polyclinic clerkship and spent the very long free time pointlessly. If you do not do even what you can do in Japanese in Japan, there is no way you can do it in a foreign language abroad. This study abroad made me realise that students' awareness of learning and their eagerness to make full use of this environment should be valued. I feel that making active use of the environment of Japan and selling its goodness abroad should be my goal from now on. It is easy to say proactivity, but it is essential to keep a more eager attitude toward learning from now on, and I feel that when I too am in the position of teaching, it will be important to approach education with that attitude.

Finally, living in a foreign country outside the clerkships was also a good experience that cannot be put into words. Going to NY twice is something that will not happen very often in the rest of my life. I intend to make an effort so that this experience does not remain a mere experience. Lastly, I quietly pray that my juniors will have fruitful and beneficial study abroad experiences for themselves. I am truly grateful to the professors of the International Collaboration Office, the alumni of the Frontier-kai, the Student Affairs staff, the laboratory that looked after me for the study abroad, the doctors of the Nagoya University Second Department of Surgery at JHU, my parents, and 布施君, who got through the nine weeks with me. Thank you.
